Separately, expanding W_n over permutations and decomposing a permutation into disjoint cycles makes its Fourier transform factor cyclewise. spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: An analytic overlap integral is converted into the range of a closed walk, and that range is then counted through convex-envelope blocks. This is the decisive representation change: shifted interval intersections become a piecewise-linear walk statistic, while Spitzer rotations and cycle counts turn that statistic into the factorially weighted subset expression required by the partition calculation.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: For an ordering theta of zero-sum increments u_j, the consecutive sums define a closed walk with range V(theta)=M(theta)-m(theta). Because f_2 is the indicator of [-1/2,1/2], the integral of its shifted copies is the length of an interval intersection, equal under the support condition to 1-V. Summing V over cyclic orderings gives T. After reducing by continuity to generic u, Spitzer's unique-rotation lemma and the upper convex envelope decompose every ordered walk into blocks below chords with decreasing slopes. The resulting bijection counts block orderings by factorials; summing the block contributions and pairing a subset with its complement proves the subset formula for T and hence Proposition 4.3.
directed.conceptual_reading: The walk representation compresses many interval endpoints into two extrema. Rotation invariance removes an arbitrary starting point, and the upper convex envelope supplies a canonical decomposition whose blocks can be reconstructed uniquely from partition data plus cyclic orderings. Thus a geometric extremum statistic becomes a partition sum, completing the semantic bridge between Fourier overlap and Möbius weights.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge runs from shifted intervals to partial sums, then to the range V, the cyclic sum T, upper-convex-envelope blocks satisfying the two Spitzer properties, and finally set partitions whose complementary permutations are counted through disjoint cycles.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The argument assumes sum u_j=0 and sum |u_j|<2; without the support condition the claimed interval length need not be 1-V. Genericity is used for uniqueness and is removed only by continuity. The unit relies on Spitzer's lemma and proves the stated subset identity, not a broader random-walk principle outside these hypotheses.

Instead of completing the harder local integral or unitary-dual analysis, the proof imports global holomorphy to exclude poles at or beyond one. The unit therefore contains an explicit method-selection lesson: use the global object when it constrains the local obstruction more cheaply.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Real square-integrable building blocks occur only in degrees one and two: characters and twists of discrete series. Their principal factors are Gamma_R or Gamma_C factors, and duplication rewrites the full archimedean factor as a product of m Gamma_R(s+mu_pi(j)). Basic Rankin-Selberg products for characters, signs, and discrete series, combined with the Langlands-quotient product, show that the first local self Rankin-Selberg pole occurs at 2 max |Re s_j|. For a real component of a cuspidal automorphic representation, the stated global Rankin-Selberg holomorphy forces that pole below one, hence the one-half bound and Re mu_pi(j)>-1/2.
directed.conceptual_reading: Gamma shifts provide coordinates in which local non-temperedness becomes pole position. The proof then selects between two routes: a purely local classification/integral analysis and a global-to-local obstruction argument. The latter preserves the needed pole information while avoiding a more elaborate local proof.

It proves the baseline one-half bound; the stronger bounds mentioned next require global considerations, and the later archimedean improvement is not proved in this unit.
directed.uncertainty: The strategy and classification are clear, but individual Gamma shifts and discrete-series tensor-product formulas are extraction-sensitive and should be checked against the PDF.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Global positivity is fed back into every local place. Landau's theorem bounds nonnegative Rankin-Selberg coefficients; evaluating those bounds on arbitrarily high prime powers amplifies the largest local parameter until it can no longer hide among the others. The same mechanism reaches ramified places through the earlier twist-class square lower bound, producing a uniform improved exponent.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: For the global self Rankin-Selberg series, nonnegative coefficients plus its meromorphic continuation, Gamma-factor degree data, and poles at zero and one allow Landau's theorem to give a summatory asymptotic and a pointwise coefficient bound. At an unramified prime, the relation between b(p^e) and the squared power sum of the local parameters bounds those sums for every e; passing through high powers yields |alpha_pi(p,j)|<=p^{1/2-1/(m^2+1)}. At ramified primes, Lemma 5.1 supplies the needed square lower bounds along multiples of r_l, giving the same control on the real Langlands parameters and hence on the principal local roots. A matching-looking spherical archimedean estimate is cited from another method.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is a local-global feedback loop. Positivity lets a global average theorem become pointwise coefficient control, and prime-power amplification converts coefficient growth into a spectral-radius bound on each local parameter. The ramified argument works because the twist-class representation retained a noncancelling square certificate.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is global Dirichlet coefficients b(n), their Landau growth bound, prime-power coefficients b(p^e), power sums of unramified local roots or squared twist-class sums at ramified primes, and finally the local Langlands parameters in the principal factor.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The conclusion depends on the stated analytic continuation, Gamma-factor data, pole structure, and coefficient positivity. The infinity statement is only cited, is restricted here to spherical pi_infinity, and is not established by the displayed finite-place proof. The extracted typography of the exponent is damaged.
directed.uncertainty: The argument supports the exponent 1/2-1/(m^2+1) through both finite-place cases, but its displayed fractions and epsilon exponents should be checked in the retained PDF. The archimedean analogue has citation rather than proof status in this span.
